briefs.headline: Carbon pricing relief for Indian exporters to UK
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: In a boost for businesses, the UK has agreed to recognize India’s carbon credit trading scheme, which will enable exporters to avoid “double taxation".
Officials said that the UK treasury has agreed to govt’s argument and decided to exempt goods as the Indian system was found to be meeting the qualifying criteria under the carbon border adjustment mechanism.
The decision will come as a gain for govt, which was trying to include carbon tax in the trade negotiations but the UK authorities did not agree to the proposal at that time. Besides, armed with the exemption, govt will make a fresh bid for a similar dispensation in the European Union where a trade deal has been finalized and is expected to be operationalized next year.
While the indicative list is being released by the UK treasury in individual cases there may be issues that will need to be sorted out. Officials said that relief that can be claimed by an exporter will depend on the effective carbon price that the product faces and the entity will need to explain to authorities in the UK the extent of levy that has been paid.
CBAM is a carbon pricing tool on imported goods designed to equalize carbon costs and prevent carbon leakage. While companies in the UK and EU face the tax, the mechanism is meant to ensure level-playing field. However, if a company bears a carbon pricing burden in the home market, it has to be factored in by authorities in the UK and EU, businesses have argued.

briefs.headline: India Inc business confidence rises sharply in Q2 FY27: CII survey
briefs.deck: Indian business confidence improved significantly in the second quarter of fiscal year twenty twenty-seven. Companies anticipate stronger domestic demand and increased hiring in the coming months. Capacity utilization is expected to rise, potentially encouraging private sector investment. Cost pressures showed some moderation, offering relief to corporate margins. Businesses remain cautious about…
briefs.bodyText:
Business confidence among Indian companies improved sharply in the second quarter of FY27, with firms expecting stronger demand, higher capacity utilisation and increased hiring despite continuing global uncertainties, according to a Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) survey.
The CII Business Confidence Index rose to 66.0 in the April-June quarter from 60.8 in the preceding three months, with the improvement led by companies' expectations of better business conditions ahead.
The Expectation Index, which measures the outlook for the coming quarter, jumped to 67.7 from 60.6. The Current Situation Index, meanwhile, rose to 62.6 from 61.2, indicating that expectations are improving faster than assessments of current conditions.
The findings are based on the 136th Round of CII's Quarterly Business Outlook Survey, which drew responses from more than 240 companies across sectors, regions and different firm sizes.
The stronger outlook is being reflected in expectations for domestic demand. About 61% of respondents expect demand to increase in Q2FY27, while only 9.6 per cent foresee a decline. The share expecting demand to grow by more than 20 per cent also increased to 16 per cent from 12.9 per cent in the previous quarter.
Companies are consequently preparing for higher production. The proportion expecting capacity utilisation to exceed 80% in the second half of 2026 rose to 51.6 per cent, from 36.6 per cent for the first half. CII said sustained high utilisation could encourage private-sector investment in the coming quarters.
Hiring plans also point to stronger business activity, with 53 per cent of respondents expecting to expand their workforce in Q2FY27.
The survey comes against the backdrop of stronger-than-expected economic growth. India's real GDP expanded 7.8 per cent in Q1FY27, compared with 6.9 per cent in the corresponding quarter of the previous fiscal, according to MoSPI. Manufacturing grew 9.2 per cent, while services recorded 10 per cent growth.
Chandrajit Banerjee, Director General, CII, said, "The optimism shown by businesses, as reflected in the BCI, is a clear testament to the inherent resilience of the Indian economy even as the geopolitical uncertainty continues. The steady improvement in business activity, backed by robust domestic demand and stable macroeconomic indicators, reinforces the perception that the government's facilitative policies will support a faster expansion in output and new orders, creating fresh opportunities for firms in India and abroad."
Cost pressures also showed some moderation. The share of companies expecting input costs to rise fell to 61.1 per cent in Q2FY27 from nearly two-thirds in the previous quarter, potentially offering some relief to corporate margins.
However, businesses remain cautious about external risks. Global trade uncertainty was identified as the biggest risk over the next six months, followed by volatility in commodity prices.
"Industry sentiment has turned a corner, and this is no coincidence," Banerjee said. "When business confidence, macroeconomic indicators and ground-level activity move in tandem, they point to a growth cycle that is increasingly broad-based, durable and sustainable."
Overall, the survey points to strengthening confidence among Indian businesses, with robust domestic demand, investment intentions and hiring plans supporting the growth outlook even as global trade and commodity-related risks remain.

stories.headline: ‘Pakistan has gone back 10 years’: Saeed Ajmal launches scathing PCB attack
stories.deck: Saeed Ajmal, the former spinner from Pakistan, has voiced serious concerns regarding the Pakistan Cricket Board's management, asserting that it has demoralized players and stunted their development. He also shifted blame towards Aaqib Javed and Mike Hesson for the team's ongoing struggles. Meanwhile, the PCB chairman has stood firm in his justification of recent adjustments following a Test loss…
stories.bodyText:
Former 
Pakistan
 spinner 
Saeed Ajmal
 has launched another scathing attack on the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB), accusing the governing body of playing a major role in the national team's recent struggles.
Ajmal, who claimed 362 wickets across international cricket for Pakistan before his career was brought to an early end by an issue with his bowling action, has repeatedly expressed his frustration with the PCB. The former spinner has maintained that the board failed to support him during a difficult phase of his career.
His latest criticism comes after Pakistan suffered another heavy defeat against England in the Lord's Test. Following the loss, the PCB made a series of sweeping changes, sacking head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and bowling coach Umar Gul while also sending seven players back home.
Among those sent back was Imam-ul-Haq, who did not bat in either innings and was subsequently accused of faking his calf injury.
PCB chairman Mohsin Naqvi later attempted to defend the players and urged critics to stop demotivating the team. Ajmal, however, questioned the sincerity of that message and instead accused the board itself of undermining Pakistan's cricketers.
"The board itself has demotivated the players more than anyone else. The board is not letting any player stand. There are players who have done well, who have also been dropped. There are players who have been humiliated by the PCB," Ajmal said.
Ajmal points finger at Aaqib Javed, Mike Hesson
The former Pakistan spinner also directed his criticism towards Director High Performance and selector Aaqib Javed and white-ball head coach Mike Hesson.
With Hesson also asked to take charge of the Test side for the third match against England, Ajmal claimed the pair have significant control over Pakistan cricket and held them responsible for the team's current situation.
"Aaqib Javed and Mike Hesson (who has been asked to take over the Test team for the third Test) are a team. These two are controlling everything and are responsible for this whole mess. The whole issue is about egos," Ajmal said on Samaa TV.
Ajmal further criticised the PCB's long-term planning, claiming Pakistan's cricket structure had regressed considerably.
"Our team has gone back 10 years. We have not planned for the future," he added.
Pakistan have already surrendered the Test series against England and are now facing the prospect of a clean sweep. The third and final Test is scheduled to begin at Edgbaston on Wednesday, with Hesson set to take charge of the Test side.
Mohsin Naqvi defends PCB's decision to make changes
Naqvi, meanwhile, had earlier attempted to explain the reasoning behind the PCB's decision to make such extensive changes after the Lord's defeat.
Speaking to Geo Network, the PCB chairman insisted that the decisions were not motivated by personal issues and said the board had little choice when players were not producing results.
"Every match of a series is important for us, and we are not left with any option if a player is not performing but to look for his replacement. The purpose behind these changes is not to axe players from contention, but just to replace them. Consider [Salman] Agha, who is a very good player, but he could not click because of some reasons. He was spoken to about it," he said.
Naqvi's comments were aimed at stressing that the changes should not be viewed as permanent exclusions or personal vendettas.
Ajmal, however, has taken a markedly different view, arguing that the PCB's repeated decisions to remove players and coaches have contributed to instability within the Pakistan team.
With Pakistan now one defeat away from an England series whitewash, the pressure on the board, coaching staff and players has intensified further.

stories.headline: Osaka takes major title wait in stride after U.S. Open exit
stories.deck: Despite encouraging results since returning to the tour, including ‌a U.S. Open semi-final and Wimbledon quarter-final, Osaka ‌said ⁠so much had happened in her life ⁠that the drought felt both long and short.
stories.bodyText:
Naomi Osaka's fourth-round U.S. Open defeat on Monday extended her wait for another Grand Slam title. Still, she put the setback into perspective, saying motherhood and life beyond tennis had changed how she viewed success.
The Japanese player won the last of her four major titles at the Australian Open in 2021, before stepping away from the sport and giving birth to daughter Shai three years ago.
Despite encouraging results since returning to the tour, including a U.S. Open semi-final and Wimbledon quarter-final, Osaka said so much had happened in her life that the drought felt both long and short.
"I had a kid, you know? There's a lot that happened in that time," Osaka said after her 6-1 6-4 defeat by Elena Rybakina.
"If I reflect on my career and the things I've been able to do, there's nothing that I regret or there's nothing that I'm sad about.
"If I win another Grand Slam, it's not going to change my life. That's crazy that I can say that, because I remember the first slam that I won, it was a huge whirlwind. I think it wouldn't feel as long."
Osaka won her first Grand Slam title at the U.S. Open in 2018, repeating the feat in 2020. She claimed another major at Melbourne Park in 2019.
The 28-year-old, who had to manage an Achilles injury in her loss to Rybakina on Monday, said she was continuing to learn from her defeats.
"Today, if I was to say I'm sad, I was just sad that I couldn't push off on my foot. I'm sad that I couldn't do what I had set out to do," she added.
"If I think about my life, my daughter is healthy, everyone in my family is great. I had an opportunity to play this slam. I got as far as I could. So it's only up from here."

stories.headline: CWG bronze medalist Seema Kaliramna eyes Olympics push at Asian Games
stories.deck: Seema Kaliramna returned to competition 11 months after giving birth to her son Rudra, after dealing with severe arthritis that left her unable to walk 10 metres or pick up her child. With husband and coach Ravinder by her side, she rebuilt her fitness and confidence, moving from 57.19m in 2024 to a 59.73m personal best this year and a Commonwealth Games bronze. Now, the Asian Games offer another…
stories.bodyText:
The 57.44m throw in Bhubaneswar last month did not quite match the 59.73m that Seema Kaliramna had produced two months earlier. Nor did she seem particularly bothered by it.
The Bhubaneswar competition was the World Athletics Silver Level Continental Tour meet at Kalinga Stadium on August 22, her first competition after the Commonwealth Games bronze in Glasgow.
In the women's discus, Commonwealth Games champion Samantha Hall was in the field along with Thailand's Subenrat Insaeng and Brazil's Andressa de Morais. De Morais won with 58.66m, Hall threw 58.43m, Subenrat 58.33m, and Seema finished fourth with 57.44m.
Her personal best had come at the National Inter-State Championships in June earlier this year, where she also crossed the Asian Games qualifying mark of 55.48m. A month later in Glasgow, she won Commonwealth Games bronze with 58.65m.
Now, with the Asian Games approaching, the 27-year-old discus thrower is not putting a target distance on what comes next.
“I just want to throw the discus as far as I can. Now, it can be 60, it can be 65, it can be 70 metres, sir. Now, whether I get the medal or not, that's another story, sir. I just want to do my best, sir,” Seema told Timesofindia.com in an exclusive interaction ahead of the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, which begin on September 19.
The 60m mark is still to come in competition, but Seema is in no hurry to force it, in fact, she laughs off the temptation to chase it too quickly.
Seema Kaliramna (Image credit: Special arrangement)
“It's better if we progress slowly. If we progress completely, it gets a little messy.”
Her coach and husband, Ravinder ‘Monu’ Kaliramna, has been working along the same lines. The plan was always to use the CWG as part of the build-up, with the Asian Games in mind.
Seema's own assessment after the 57.44m throw was similarly measured.
“It is not that bad. According to the Asian Games, it is good.”
From 54-55m in training to 59.73m
That calmness took time to build. Seema was preparing for the World University Games after her marriage in 2019 and says she was throwing 54-55m in training. A knee injury and then COVID kept her away from competition. She continued training around the same distance but could not get the competitions she needed.
Then came pregnancy and childbirth.
Seema gave birth to her son Rudra in 2022. He is now four years old. She returned to competitive competition 11 months after his birth, but the period around pregnancy and childbirth had left her dealing with severe physical problems.
After giving birth, Seema's physical problems became severe. She has described how her shoulder and hip had become frozen during pregnancy and how the condition worsened after delivery. Doctors told her she had severe arthritis.
“At that time, I was not able to walk up to 10 meters, and I was not able to pick up my child.”
At one point, she wondered whether continuing to live like that was possible.
“In such a condition, a person thinks that instead of living like this, it is better not to live.”
She had not simply stopped throwing, but she had to work out whether her body could return to the sport at all. Ravinder's answer was to start again, but according to her body.
“My husband said that we will start the game again. We will take her according to her body, as and when the muscle develops, the arthritis will reduce.”
It did.
Seema returned to competition in 2024. Her competition best before motherhood had been 48.08m. She went to 57.19m in 2024, won the 2025 National Games, and then moved beyond 59m this season.
Seema's return to the throwing circle was not something she worked through on her own.
Ravinder was there as her coach, but he was also the person beside her through pregnancy, the arthritis that followed and the long process of getting her body ready to compete again. The two have also been working towards the same Olympic goal. For Seema, that makes it difficult to separate the two roles.
Seema Kaliramna (Image credit: Special arrangement)
“When you have a goal, when you are living a dream… we are living the same dream, so there is not much difference between us.”
The support behind Seema's comeback
Their sporting set-up has also been supported by the Inspire Institute of Sport, which has provided Seema with physiotherapy, massage, travel, accommodation and other support.
“We don't even have a government job, we don't even have a private job, so from physio, to massage, to travelling, accommodation, everything is done by IIS. I have got full support from IIS,” Seema said.
However, there was some movement on that front recently. At a Haryana government programme in Panchkula on August 26, Seema said she was approached about a junior coach's position.
For now, though, the discus remains the priority. So does Rudra, even when he is not at the stadium.
Rudra will watch from home again
Before the CWG, Seema had spoken about how difficult it was to leave her son behind. In Glasgow, she won bronze and then spoke about missing him. Before she left for the CWG, Seema knew what Rudra was hoping she would bring back - a medal; and she did.
He will not be travelling with her to the Asian Games either.
A medal will make the trip back home again, just as it did after the CWG. Seema hopes that, one day, Rudra will be the one travelling to competitions - and that she and Monu will be the ones going with him.
Seema Kaliramna and son Rudra (Image credit: Special arrangement)
“He cannot go with me now, but we will make him [raise him in a way] so that in the future he goes out and we go with him.”
For now, Rudra will again watch from home, and Seema will go back into the circle, with a CWG bronze behind her, a 59.73m personal best beside her name and an Asian Games medal somewhere ahead.
And she is already thinking beyond that. After winning at Glasgow, her first reaction was not about the distance or the podium. Instead, it was: “We did it.”
Now she wants the Asian Games to be another step. “So, we will climb one more step towards the Olympics after winning a medal at the Asian Games.”

stories.headline: Blockx first Belgian man to reach U.S. Open quarter-finals
stories.deck: The win marks the latest stepping stone for Blockx, who began the year outside the top 100 and had to qualify for the Australian Open.
stories.bodyText:
Alexander Blockx beat Francisco Cerundolo in four sets on Monday (September 7, 2026) to become the first Belgian man ever to reach the U.S. Open quarter-finals.
The 21-year-old Blockx, seeded 28th in his Flushing Meadows debut, out-lasted 24th-seeded Cerundolo 6-3, 4-6, 7-5, 7-5.
Blockx, who upset fifth-seeded Flavio Cobolli in the third round, backed up that win with a determined performance during which he received "magical medication" from the doctor to combat a "sharp pain in my rib.
"I was just holding on to be honest," Blockx said. "Even though I won that first set 6-3, it could have been the other way round."
The win marks the latest stepping stone for Blockx, who began the year outside the top 100 and had to qualify for the Australian Open.
After splitting the first two sets, Blockx and Cerundolo stood level at 5-5 when the Belgian fell behind 0-40 on his serve.
Blockx worked his way back with big serves and booming strokes, holding serve and breaking Cerundolo in the next game to take the third set.
A tight fourth set went with serve until Blockx gained the winning break in the final game, falling to the ground in delight when a shot from the Argentine landed out.
"This morning I stepped onto this court for the first time to warm up and that felt unreal, so to play a match here and win a match here is even crazier," Blockx said
Blockx next faces the winner between unseeded Russian Karen Khachanov and 14th-seeded Learner Tien of the United States.

briefs.headline: Rybakina thumps Osaka to reach U.S. Open quarters, close in on top ranking
briefs.deck: The flawless victory for Rybakina, who won Wimbledon ‌in 2022 and this year's Australian Open, booked a last-eight clash with ‌Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen and left ‌the ⁠Kazakh one match win away from ⁠becoming world number one for the first time.
briefs.bodyText:
Elena Rybakina cleared another big hurdle in her bid to win a third Grand Slam title by outclassing former U.S. Open champion Naomi Osaka 6-1 6-4 on Monday (September 7, 2026) to reach the quarter-finals at Flushing Meadows.
The flawless victory for Rybakina, who won Wimbledon in 2022 and this year's Australian Open, booked a last-eight clash with Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen and left the Kazakh one match win away from becoming world number one for the first time.
Second seed Rybakina raced through the opening set in 22 minutes, converting two of her three break-point opportunities before sealing it with a booming serve to leave two-times New York champion Osaka on the ropes at Louis Armstrong Stadium.
The 13th-seeded Osaka, who had arrived in style in a fur-collared overcoat that featured oversized signage, a mural-like city scene and a portrait, showed greater resistance early in the second set, but Rybakina soon seized control again.
Osaka clutched her left leg at 2-2 in the second set, still feeling the effects of an Achilles niggle that flared up in the third round, but the 28-year-old managed to save a break point and stay in the fight.
Rybakina continued to heap pressure on Osaka with her deep groundstrokes and earned the decisive break in the seventh game when her Japanese opponent hit a forehand into the net, before she closed out the match in 66 minutes.

briefs.headline: Ballon D'Or: Mbappé says he would vote for himself; cites World Cup record
briefs.deck: Real Madrid star Kylian Mbappé believes he has a genuine chance of winning the Ballon d’Or, despite lacking major team silverware. He says his individual achievements, including his World Cup Golden Boot and goalscoring record, strengthen his case. Asked who he would vote for, Mbappé confidently chose himself while acknowledging other voters may disagree.
briefs.bodyText:
Kylian Mbappé has made it clear he has no intention of playing down his chances of winning the Ballon d'Or.
The Real Madrid striker believes his individual achievements give him a genuine shot at claiming the prestigious award, despite the lack of major team silverware during the season under consideration.
And when asked who he would vote for, Mbappé had a typically confident answer.
Mbappé insists he would vote for himself
Mbappé's comments came in a preview of an interview with France Football, with the full conversation due to be broadcast in the coming period.
Speaking to 
Marca
 hours before the announcement of the 30 nominees for the 70th edition of the award, Mbappé said he still sees himself as a serious contender.
“I have a feeling that I am capable of winning it this year, and that is why I have not moved away from this goal,” the France international said.
Mbappé described the Ballon d'Or as one of his main short-term objectives and based much of his argument on the fact that it is an individual award.
“It is an individual award, and what the player has produced at an individual level is what is considered,” he said.
Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe celebrates after scoring his sides third goal during the La Liga soccer match between Real Madrid and Malaga in Madrid, Spain, Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)
The forward also addressed the criticism that his candidacy should be weakened by his lack of collective honours.
“People say I have not won titles, but I have never seen a unanimous Ballon d'Or given to a player who achieved everything every time,” Mbappé said.
“I do not know if there has ever been a player who won it with 100% of the votes, and that means there is always someone who feels he did not deserve it.”
When the conversation turned to his own ballot, there was no hesitation.
“Who will I vote for? Myself.”
Mbappé immediately acknowledged that other voters are entitled to reach a different conclusion.
“But I understand those who vote differently, we are not in a dictatorship of thought,” he added.
“When I look at the arguments, and when I look at the competition, I tell myself that my winning the award would not be a theft.”
Mbappé points to his World Cup record
The strongest part of Mbappé's case is the individual record he produced at the World Cup.
He finished the tournament as its top scorer and won the Golden Boot, giving him a major achievement to put alongside his goalscoring numbers.
“To become the all-time top scorer at the World Cup, and to surpass all the great legends of the sport throughout history in the most important tournament in existence, is something that draws attention, a global event,” Mbappé said.
He also argued that finishing as the leading scorer in the biggest competitions should carry significant weight when the award is decided.
“To finish major competitions as top scorer, where the best players in the world take part, is important,” he said. “History must always be rewarded.”
However, there is an obvious complication to Mbappé's candidacy.
Real Madrid finished the season without major silverware, while France also failed to lift the World Cup. That leaves Mbappé's impressive individual achievements competing against a traditional factor in the Ballon d'Or race: what a player actually won with his team.
The award's assessment period runs until July 19, the day Spain were crowned World Cup winners against Argentina.
Spain midfielder Rodri was named the tournament's best player, putting him among the most prominent rivals to Mbappé in the race.
France Football is due to announce its 30 nominees for the 70th edition of the Ballon d'Or, with the ceremony scheduled for October 26 in London.
There is no obvious runaway favourite this year, which is precisely why Mbappé believes his individual record deserves to put him in the conversation.
He knows the absence of major titles will count against him.
But if the question is whether Mbappé believes he belongs in the race, his answer could hardly be clearer.
He would vote for himself.

briefs.headline: Asian Games | For cricket to grow, it has to be played everywhere: Sunil Gavaskar
briefs.deck: Though reports have emerged of the arrangements in Japan for the cricketers not being up to scratch, Gavaskar emphasised that such obstacles shouldn’t dissuade the game’s stakeholders from exploring newer markets
briefs.bodyText:
In an unrelenting cricket calendar where monotony can set in over run-of-the-mill bilateral assignments, a multi-disciplinary event like the Asian Games holds the promise of a novel offering.
The competition provides a unique opportunity for India’s high-profile cricketers to mingle with athletes from other sports whilst attempting to win gold for the nation. Shreyas Iyer & Co. will be looking to do just that when they travel to Japan for the continental spectacle’s T20 tournament from September 24 to October 3.
This will be the Indian cricket team’s second appearance at the Asian Games, having pocketed gold in Hangzhou, China, in 2023.
Sunil Gavaskar hopes the Men in Blue savour the experience of a multi-sport carnival. “You get to know and talk to athletes from other sports, and get to know what makes them tick. It will be a wonderful experience,” he said during a virtual media interaction.
Though reports have emerged of the arrangements in Japan for the cricketers not being up to scratch, Gavaskar emphasised that such obstacles shouldn’t dissuade the game’s stakeholders from exploring newer markets.
“If cricket has to become a global sport, it has to be played in different parts of the world. At the Olympics, for example, you could play in a city where cricket isn’t generally played. You might not always get the best facilities,” the 77-year-old opined. “For the game to grow, I would encourage them to play wherever possible.”
If cricket is to pique the curiosity of spectators at the Asian Games, the boy wonder that is Vaibhav Sooryavanshi will have to show up. The spunky 15-year-old, who cracked two half-centuries against Zimbabwe after a baptism by fire against England, will hope to continue his upward flight.
“Look in T20 cricket, you can’t expect consistency. Vaibhav is the kind of batter who can win you three or four out of 10 games. But he’s somebody with whom we need to have patience,” assessed Gavaskar.

briefs.headline: GCL: Knights score over Pipers
briefs.bodyText:
Viswanathan Anand rarely plays these days: he is more of a mentor and now the interim president of FIDE. Magnus Carlsen, who dethroned Anand as the World champion in 2013, has relinquished his crown.
Still, when the two all-time greats come across a chessboard, there is a buzz. That was quite palpable at the Lalit Ashok on Monday. They played some interesting chess too, on the third day of the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League, but Anand was unlucky, as he lost on time from an equal position. The five-time World champion, however, could afford to forget his defeat, as his team, PBG Alaskan Knights, won the match against Alpine APL Pipers 9-7. That, in fact, was the first loss in the tournament for Carlsen’s team after winning both their matches.
A little later, however, the defending champion bounced back, scoring a crushing 15-3 win against Fyers American Gambits. Carlsen was held to a draw by Javokhir Sindarov, but K. Humpy, Vidit Gujrathi and Volodar Murzin won their games, with black pieces, to ensure that their team would score heavily.
The Pipers top the table after four rounds. It has nine match points, and 43 game points. As many as four teams are on six points — Mumba Masters (36 game points), American Gambits (34), Alaskan Knights (30) and Ganges Grandmasters (28). briefs.headline: Shooter Suruchi brimming with excitement ahead of maiden Asiad appearance
briefs.bodyText:
Suruchi Phogat first held a pistol in 2019, at the age of 13. She did so because there were no rifles at the Guru Dronacharya Shooting Academy in Bhiwani; and because her father was determined to make her a sportsperson.
The 20-year-old will be one of the favourites to medal for India in 10m air pistol at the Asian Games later this month, as much because of her performance streak over the past 18 months as her ability to keep things simple. “Excitement. No nervousness, no challenge, nothing. There is only excitement inside me because it is my first Asian Games,” she said, a permanent wide smile on her face exuding an openness that only accentuates her clarity of thought.
The ‘baby’ of the Indian shooting contingent, Suruchi insisted everyone’s equal in the squad but admitted that certain members of the coaching and sports science staff are slightly more protective, telling her what to do and expect while travelling.
It is a throwback to the time she took the local trains for a 100-km journey from Sasroli village in Jhajjar district of Haryana to the academy.
“My father and brother accompanied me. At that time, of course no one knew but once the results and medals started coming, the regulars on the train would recognise me. They would say they had seen my face in the local newspapers and be curious. I would tell them that I am a shooter. It’s not like I suddenly became famous or anything but yes, it was the beginning of a realisation that I am doing something,” she laughed.
Making the cut for Nagoya has been an eventful journey that has seen her win four consecutive World Cups and the World Cup Final, set a National record in 10m air pistol and a World Junior Record in the process and rise to World No. 3. It is only the beginning.

briefs.headline: ‘It’s always Plan A’ for Satwik-Chirag
briefs.deck: Their 10th crown on the BWF World Tour gives them a timely confidence boost heading into their Asian Games title defence later this month
briefs.bodyText:
Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, down a game and staring at a third runner-up finish, tore up the script. They stormed back to beat home favourites He Ji Ting and Ren Xiang Yu 11-21, 21-13, 21-17 on Sunday, avenging two painful final losses in 2023 and 2025 to finally win the China Masters.
Satwik credited the win to a marked improvement in their physical conditioning, coming just weeks after a disappointing quarterfinal exit at the badminton World championships at home. “We weren’t sure how our bodies could cope throughout the week in China. But we became much better after the World championships. Our bodies settled down, and we got better. That’s a good sign going forward,” Satwik said during a virtual interaction on Monday.
Chirag added that the physical grind of their run in China had doubled as ideal preparation — mentally and physically — for the final itself.
Through it all, the attack-minded duo remained committed to their game plan. “It’s always Plan A; there is no Plan B for us,” Satwik emphasised.
“The Chinese want to play a fast game, and if you’re playing with Malaysians and Indonesians, they’re not as attacking,” he explained, while also crediting his partner for the pair’s attacking edge.
Their 10th crown on the BWF World Tour gives them a timely confidence boost heading into their Asian Games title defence later this month.
Meanwhile, Chirag, spotted with a belt strapped around his waist during the post-match celebrations, was quick to wave off any fitness concerns ahead of the continental event.
“I’ve been wearing it since the injury at the All England last year. If I get a period of one month, probably in December, when I can have a good stretch of practice, that is when I can try playing without it and see how I feel. Not confident enough until then,” he stressed.

briefs.headline: 'Shenzhen win has given us confidence': Satwik-Chirag turn focus to Asian Games
briefs.deck: Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty overcame injuries and a deficit to win their maiden China Masters title, defeating China's He Ji Ting and Ren Xiang Yu in Shenzhen. The victory erased the disappointment of their World Championships collapse, restored confidence in Satwik's recovering shoulder, and provided timely momentum before they defend their Asian Games gold.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Satwiksairaj Rankireddy
 and 
Chirag Shetty
 have built a reputation for doing things the hard way. They fall behind, regroup, and more often than not, find a way back.
On Sunday in Shenzhen, that familiar script delivered one of their most important victories of the season. The Indian pair rallied from a set down to defeat China's He Ji Ting and Ren Xiang Yu 11-21, 21-13, 21-17 and lift their maiden China Masters Super 750 title, ending a run of two previous final defeats at the tournament.
The triumph was significant beyond the trophy. Just two weeks earlier, Satwik and Chirag had walked away from the World Championships in New Delhi devastated after surrendering a winning position in the quarterfinals. Even their participation in China had been uncertain, with Satwik continuing to manage a chronic shoulder injury and Chirag still wearing support for his lower back - something he's been handling for a-year-and-half.
Five grueling matches later, they were back on top of the podium.
'Shenzhen gives us confidence'
The China Masters has been a curious constant in the Indians' career. They had finished runners-up in 2023 and 2025, but the venue has repeatedly produced some of their strongest performances, even when arriving short of preparation or confidence.
"We weren't thinking about the fact that we have lost two times in the final there. We were thinking that we have played two finals there. It is kind of like the French Open for us -- we feel very comfortable, stadium feels good, atmosphere feels good," Satwik said.
The 26-year-old pointed to a string of encouraging campaigns in Shenzhen across difficult phases of their career.
"Even this year, we were coming back from injury, wanted confidence and Shenzhen has given that. We always go with the same intent. Whenever we get a chance, we grab that. Only concern was whether body is cooperating or not, if it is not, we wanted to take a step back because of Asian Games but pretty much confident throughout the week," Satwik said.
That confidence was tested almost immediately in the final. The Chinese pair dominated the opening game with relentless flat exchanges that prevented the Indians from generating attacking opportunities — a tactical pattern that has troubled them before.
But unlike the World Championships, where Satwik's shoulder visibly limited his overhead game, the Indian pair gradually wrestled control of the rallies. They accepted the lifts, dictated the mid-court and allowed Satwik's attack to come alive again. The comeback followed.
The difference from World Championships
The transformation, both insisted, was more physical than mental. "I think it was mainly physical. I think we became much better after the World Championships. We got time, we got off and adjusted," Satwik said.
The unusual scheduling of the BWF calendar — with a mandatory Super 750 event two weeks after the World Championships and another fortnight before the Asian Games — had left little room for recovery in Delhi.
"The World Championship was difficult for us because we didn't have much time (on the court). We played one match, then we played quarterfinals right away. So I think after (the) World Championship, our body kind of gets settled down, used to it. Then we kind of got better. Then we weren't sure as well in China Masters, like how much we can cope up with the body throughout the week. So we just took it one match at a time. So I think overall it was pretty much comfortable throughout the week. That's a good sign going ahead," Satwik said.
Chirag echoed that assessment, saying the lack of match rhythm had hurt them more than anything at the World Championships.
"At the World Championships, we didn't really get a lot of court time as such, especially going into a tough match in the quarterfinals against the Chinese. And we were playing a tournament after almost three odd months. And the first match that we played was very scratchy. I think our body didn't cope as well," Chirag said.
The contrast was evident in China. Except for the opening round, every match went the distance, forcing the Indians to endure four three-game contests in succession.
"Whereas when we played five matches here at the China Open, and we almost played three sets, barring the first round, we played four three sets. And yet I think the body feels a lot better than it was at the World Championship. So I think we got another week of practice going towards the China Masters. That really helped us to do well," Chirag said.
Perfect timing before Asian Games
The focus for the duo now shifts to Japan and the Asian Games, which will be held in Aichi-Nagoya from September 19, where the Indians will defend both their men's doubles gold and India's team silver.
"We have 10 days to go before we head to Japan. And today was an off day. Obviously, we came only early this morning, so we couldn't really sleep as much. So tomorrow we are back on court training for the Asian Games," Chirag said.
